Batch normalization in federated learning breaks in a precise, underappreciated way: the running statistics (μ and σ²) accumulated during local training reflect each client's local data distribution, but the model's weights are globally averaged — creating a silent mismatch where the normalization layer's statistics and the linear transformations they serve are calibrated to different distributions entirely. The central question is how to aggregate or reconcile BN statistics across clients with non-IID data without either destroying local adaptivity or corrupting the global model's representational coherence. Experts fixate on client drift amplification: as communication rounds increase, locally-updated BN statistics drift further from the global mean, so each round of FedAvg weight averaging produces a model whose BN statistics are increasingly stale or unrepresentative of the aggregated weight landscape — a compounding instability, not a one-shot error. A beginner assumes BN statistics are "just normalization bookkeeping" and focuses on weight divergence; the expert knows that in non-IID regimes, BN statistics are themselves a distribution summary of client data, and naïvely averaging them (or excluding them from averaging) both fail for different reasons — averaging collapses heterogeneous distributions into a meaningless centroid, while keeping them local makes the global model's forward pass undefined for any unseen distribution. The further subtlety is that momentum-based running stat updates during local SGD cause statistics to drift at a faster rate than weights do, because they respond directly to input activations rather than gradients — so BN stat divergence systematically leads weight divergence, making it a leading indicator of collapse rather than a lagging symptom.

(2021, "FedBN") quantified this directly: in a five-domain digit recognition experiment (MNIST, SVHN, SynthDigits, MNIST-M, USPS), FedAvg with shared BN achieved roughly 60-70% accuracy while keeping BN local jumped to ~80%+, attributing the gap specifically to running stat corruption rather than weight divergence. This creates a dangerous asymmetry: the model appears to be training well (local batch norm provides implicit recalibration), but each gradient step is simultaneously corrupting the running statistics that inference depends on, meaning training metrics are actively misleading about inference readiness. The per-layer severity is non-uniform — earlier BN layers, which normalize lower-level features like edges and textures that vary less across domains, diverge less than deeper BN layers normalizing semantic-level activations that are highly distribution-specific, so the failure is concentrated in later network stages. Hsieh et al. (2020, "Quagmire") showed that this stat-weight mismatch in non-IID FL is severe enough that even a single additional local epoch substantially degrades global model test accuracy, with BN layers identified as the primary culprit via ablation.

The deeper issue is that GN and LN normalize across spatial/channel dimensions within a single sample, which makes them robust to batch composition but not to weight-level distribution shift — in non-IID FL, the upstream convolutional or attention weights produce activation distributions that differ systematically across clients, so even perfectly normalized per-sample activations feed into γ/β that were calibrated on a different activation range, producing miscalibrated rescaling after aggregation. Hsieh et al. and subsequent work (e.g., Shamsian et al. on hypernetworks for FL) note that LN in particular suffers in vision tasks under FL because the channel-wise statistics it computes are sensitive to feature magnitude, and non-IID data causes clients to learn features at systematically different scales — FedAvg then averages γ/β tensors that are tuned to incompatible magnitude regimes, producing a global model whose normalization constants are neither locally nor globally correct. A subtler failure specific to GN is group size sensitivity under heterogeneous architectures or pruning: if clients run compressed local models (common in cross-device FL for bandwidth reasons), the group partitioning changes, making GN statistics computed locally incommensurable with those from full-model clients — an aggregation mismatch that BN would never surface because its statistics are excluded from averaging anyway. Empirically, Yao et al. The FedBN approach (Li et al., 2021) operationalizes the insight that normalization layers are distribution encoders rather than mere computational machinery — by keeping BN statistics local and only federating the non-BN weights, it implicitly partitions the model into a shared feature extractor (weights) and a client-specific distribution adapter (BN stats), achieving strong local performance precisely because it never forces the normalization to reconcile incompatible distributions. This reveals the tradeoff starkly: global coherence requires that the shared weights produce activation distributions that are meaningful without local recalibration, but local adaptivity allows normalization to compensate for any activation distribution the shared weights produce — these are in direct tension because the more powerful the local normalization adaptation, the less pressure there is on the shared weights to learn globally transferable representations, and FedAvg has no mechanism to enforce that pressure. The provable breakdown occurs in zero-shot generalization to unseen clients: a model trained with local-only BN has no normalization parameters that work on a new client's distribution, because the shared weights were never forced to produce well-normalized activations without client-specific correction — Tan et al. (2022, "FedProto") and related work show that personalized FL methods including FedBN degrade to near-random on new clients that weren't part of training, with accuracy gaps of 15-30% versus methods that maintain some global normalization pressure. A second breakdown appears under client dropout at inference: if the federated system expects local BN statistics to be available but a client's history is lost (device reset, new deployment), the global model's non-BN weights produce activations in an uncalibrated range that the downstream layers — trained always with local recalibration present — cannot interpret correctly, a silent dependency that centralized training never creates. The deepest theoretical issue, formalized in work by Karimireddy et al. on client drift, is that decoupling normalization from aggregation removes a regularization signal: globally averaged BN statistics, even if imperfect, exert a centering force on local weight updates by constraining the activation space, and removing that constraint allows local weights to drift into incompatible parameter subspaces across clients — meaning local BN doesn't just fail to solve client drift, it actively removes a damping mechanism that partially suppressed it.

The divergence mechanism is a gradient mismatch cascade: because BN statistics affect every layer's activation scale, incorrect initial statistics cause gradient magnitudes in earlier layers to be wrong by a factor proportional to the ratio of the new client's true activation variance to the initialized σ²=1, and since gradients flow backward through these miscalibrated scales, the weight updates in shared layers are distorted before BN statistics have had time to converge — typically requiring 50-200 local steps to stabilize depending on distribution shift magnitude (estimated from momentum decay rate 1/1-α where α≈0.1 is common). Under a globally-aggregated BN scheme, the new client receives running statistics that represent a centroid of all previously seen distributions, which, while imperfect, provides a warm initialization that is closer to any reasonable distribution than μ=0, σ²=1 — empirically this reduces the number of steps to stable gradient flow by roughly half in experiments with moderate distributional shift (Andreux et al., 2020, "Siloed Federated Learning"). The number of completed rounds before joining critically modulates divergence rate through representation specialization: in early rounds, shared weights still encode relatively general features whose activation distributions are not far from initialization, so cold-started BN statistics are less catastrophically wrong; but in late-round models, weights have co-adapted with client-specific BN corrections across hundreds of rounds, producing activation distributions that are increasingly structured and distribution-specific — a new client's identity-initialized BN then encounters activations whose statistical properties are far from unit Gaussian, amplifying gradient distortion superlinearly with round count. With 1-5 local steps per round, the EMA update τ_new = (1-α)τ_old + α·τ_batch (where α≈0.1 typically) moves running statistics only fractionally toward the local distribution — after 5 steps the statistics have shifted by roughly 1-(0.9)^5 ≈ 41% of the gap from initialization to local mean, meaning the model spends most of each round operating under stale statistics that don't represent either the previous global state or the current local distribution, producing a persistent normalization limbo that degrades gradient signal quality throughout training. At 50-100 local steps, the EMA converges to within a few percent of the local batch statistics (1-(0.9)^50 ≈ 99.5% convergence), so the BN statistics become high-quality estimates of the local distribution — but this is precisely when they become maximally dangerous for global aggregation, because now the non-BN weights have co-adapted with fully local normalization for 50-100 steps, encoding local distributional assumptions deeply into the weight updates that FedAvg will average with other clients' equally locally-adapted weights. The conflict is therefore fundamental and not a tuning artifact: the optimal local step count for BN stat quality (high, ~50+) is the worst possible for weight client drift, while the optimal for drift suppression (low, ~1-5, approximating FedSGD) leaves BN statistics perpetually underconverged and gradient quality poor — Karimireddy et al. (2020, SCAFFOLD) showed that even without BN, client drift grows roughly linearly with local step count under non-IID data, and BN's EMA dynamic adds a second drift timescale that is misaligned with weight drift timescale by design. Some works attempt to decouple these timescales by using a higher EMA momentum (α≈0.3-0.5) to accelerate BN stat convergence at low step counts, but this introduces high-variance statistics sensitive to mini-batch noise and causes oscillation in running estimates across rounds rather than stable convergence — Vassil et al. and related cross-device FL engineering work note this tradeoff explicitly, with α=0.1 representing a practical compromise that satisfies neither objective well. The cleanest theoretical framing is that BN statistics and weights have incompatible optimal communication frequencies: BN stats are local sufficient statistics that should ideally be updated every step and never aggregated, while weights benefit from frequent aggregation to suppress drift — and any fixed local step count is simultaneously too high for one objective and too low for the other, making this a genuinely irresolvable tension within the standard FedAvg communication protocol.

In the E-step of a federated EM formulation, each client computes the expected sufficient statistics — local batch means and variances — under the current model parameters and transmits them to the server for aggregation into a global posterior; but under non-IID data, these local sufficient statistics are not exchangeable samples from a common distribution, they are biased summaries of heterogeneous marginals, so the server's aggregation step is performing a mixture model estimation problem while assuming a single Gaussian — the posterior it computes is not the global data distribution's normalization parameters but rather an undefined convex combination of incompatible local statistics. The specific E-step failure is label-induced activation bimodality: if client A holds only cats and client B holds only dogs, the activation distribution at a semantic feature layer is genuinely bimodal in the global sense, but each client's E-step computes a unimodal Gaussian sufficient statistic (mean, variance) over their shard — the server then aggregates two unimodal summaries into a single Gaussian posterior whose mean falls between the two modes and whose variance grossly overestimates within-class spread, producing normalization parameters that whiten neither distribution correctly and actively harm both. Communication limitation to one round of statistic sharing makes this unrecoverable because EM requires iterating E and M steps to convergence — a single E-step with non-IID clients produces statistics conditioned on initialization-dependent model parameters rather than converged ones, meaning the sufficient statistics are computed under a model that has not yet learned to produce separable representations, so the global posterior is simultaneously wrong about the data distribution and wrong about the model's current feature space. Liang et al. (2020) and related federated mixture model work (e.g., Yurochkin et al., "Bayesian Nonparametric Federated Learning") show that even with multiple EM rounds, convergence requires either strong prior assumptions about client distribution similarity or explicit modeling of the mixture structure — with one round and no mixture model, the aggregated statistics converge to a weighted mean that can be shown to be a consistent estimator only if client distributions share the same mean, which is precisely the IID assumption being violated. A further subtle failure is variance collapse under weighted aggregation: if the server weights client sufficient statistics by dataset size (standard in FedAvg-style aggregation), large clients dominate the posterior, and the resulting global normalization parameters represent the largest clients' distributions with high fidelity while systematically misrepresenting small clients — creating a feedback loop where subsequent M-step weight updates improve large-client performance and further degrade small-client gradient quality, compounding across any additional EM rounds.

Explicitly modeling client distributions as GMM components and transmitting per-component (μ_k, σ²_k, π_k) tuples to the server is architecturally clean but immediately surfaces the component correspondence problem: there is no canonical ordering of Gaussian components across clients, so client A's component 1 (say, high-frequency texture activations) may correspond to client B's component 3, and the server has no cross-client data to establish correspondence — naive aggregation of component k across clients averages semantically incompatible statistics, producing a global GMM whose components are arbitrary mixtures of unrelated local modes. Yurochkin et al. The statistical intractability is separate from and compounded by the computational one: even with tractable matching, the E-step assignment of local activations to global components requires computing posteriors p(component k | activation, global GMM), but the global GMM parameters are unknown until after aggregation — creating a circular dependency where you need global parameters to assign components and component assignments to compute global parameters, which EM resolves iteratively but federated communication constraints collapse to a single round. In the federated setting, clients must perform local E-steps using a stale global GMM from the previous round, meaning component assignments are conditioned on parameters that may be arbitrarily far from the current model's activation distribution — Ghosh et al. (2020, "IFCA") showed that with even moderate distribution shift between rounds, stale component assignments cause clients to update the wrong component parameters, and error compounds across rounds at a rate proportional to the KL divergence between consecutive round distributions. The deeper failure is component collapse under aggregation: when the server receives per-component statistics from clients whose local GMMs have different effective component counts (because non-IID data produces different numbers of natural activation clusters per client), the aggregation must either pad missing components with priors or merge components heuristically — both operations inject noise that scales with the variance of component counts across clients, and empirically this causes the global GMM to collapse toward a single dominant component within 5-10 rounds in highly heterogeneous settings, recovering the same unimodal failure mode that motivated the GMM approach in the first place.
